passage:
Sahil pulled a new phone out of his bag at the bus stop and held it so the cover showed. "Got it yesterday. Also, ninety-four in physics. You?"
Keerthana had seen that quick glance after every test in their small town, checking whose face would drop. She felt a sting, then smiled. "Nice. The screen looks bright." She told him her own marks, seventy-eight, without dressing them up. "Ninety-four is a lot of work," she said, and meant it.
Then she offered him half her puffed rice from the shop by the stop. He blinked, and for a moment the game went out of him. On the bus she thought about the science-fair model she still wanted to finish, and what she cared about there.

qa.q: What marks did Sahil say he got in physics?
qa.a: He said he got ninety-four in physics.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when Sahil flashed the phone and the marks, and what did she think was behind it?
qa.a: She sensed a quick glance to see whose face would drop, as if he compared to feel better than her; it stung a little, though she stayed calm. 😔

qa.q: Which choice of Keerthana's kept the moment from becoming a contest, and why?
qa.a: She answered kindly and honestly, told her marks plainly and shared her puffed rice, so she stayed warm without competing.

qa.q: Why might Sahil have blinked when offered puffed rice?
qa.a: He may have expected a contest or a sulk, and her kindness left him unsure what to do, so the game briefly went out of him.

grounding: Shows a teen sensing a friend's flaunting as comparison, staying warm, not competing, and returning to her own interests.

passage:
In the girls' hostel of the Pune college, Afreen always had something new. A new phone. New headphones. And every time results came out, she'd lean over to Mehak's bed. "What did you get? I got 92. Oh, you got 81? That's also fine."

Mehak started to dread results day. She felt a small, tight knot every time Afreen asked. It wasn't really a question. It was a scoreboard.

She thought about buying the same headphones on her mother's money, or studying just to beat Afreen. Neither felt like her.

So on Sunday, when Afreen showed off another new watch, Mehak said, "It's nice," and meant it. When Afreen asked her marks, she said, "I'm happy with mine, thanks," and went back to her book.

That evening Afreen came back from a call with her father, eyes red. Mehak didn't ask about marks. She made two cups of instant coffee and sat on Afreen's bed. They talked till lights-out about everything except scores.

qa.q: What mark did Afreen say she got?
What was Mehak feeling each time Afreen asked about marks?
qa.a: Mehak felt a tight knot of discomfort and dread, sensing Afreen was keeping score rather than asking.

qa.q: What did Mehak do that was wise?
qa.a: Mehak stayed warm, gave a short answer without competing, and stuck to her own values instead of buying the same things or studying just to win.

qa.q: Why might Afreen keep comparing herself to Mehak?
qa.a: Afreen may feel insecure or pressured, perhaps by her father, and comparing helps her feel better for a moment.

grounding: It shows a teen whose friend keeps flashing new things and grades to feel superior, staying warm, not competing and staying grounded in her own values.

passage:
Dear Didi,

You asked on the phone why I sounded weird. It's Nikita. You remember her from my birthday.

Every day she posts something: new shoes, the new bike her uncle bought her, and her test marks with a crown emoji. Then she messages me, "What did you get? Did you see my 95?" At first I was happy for her. Now I feel like she's measuring herself against me to feel bigger.

The worst part is I started doing it back. I nearly posted my 88 with a caption to beat her. I felt petty and sick afterwards and deleted it.

I don't want that. Nikita's funny and kind when we're not talking about marks. So I've decided: I'll say "congrats" and mean it, and not share my marks online. When we meet, I'll talk about the book club and the badminton match instead.

I'm trying to remember what Amma says: know what matters to you, then the noise gets quieter.

Love,
Raghav

qa.q: What mark did Raghav nearly post?
What did Raghav feel after nearly posting the mark to beat Nikita?
qa.a: Raghav felt petty and sick, not liking the way the comparison was changing things.

qa.q: What did Raghav decide to do, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Raghav decided to congratulate Nikita sincerely, not post marks, and talk about shared interests, which keeps the friendship warm without competing.

qa.q: Why might Nikita keep posting her marks and new things?
qa.a: Nikita may feel insecure or need to feel ahead of others, so comparison gives her a quick feeling of being bigger.

grounding: It shows a teen whose friend keeps flashing new things and grades to feel better, choosing to stay warm, avoid competing and stay grounded in their own values.
